dedupe_keys.name: environmental and socioeconomic impacts of pipeline transport interdiction in the niger delta nigeria heliyon 2021

description: This case study is a 2021 Heliyon article on the environmental and economic effects of pipeline interdiction, meaning damage to crude oil pipelines, in the Niger Delta of Nigeria, where pipelines are the most economic way to move crude oil to production and distribution facilities. The authors mapped the spatial distribution of oil spills with kernel density estimation in a geographic information system, using records of Nigeria's national oil spill detection and response agency, synthesised the literature on the historical, socioeconomic and environmental effects, and analysed soil samples for hydrocarbon pollutants against uncontaminated control sites. The abstract reports that total petroleum hydrocarbon in impacted soil ranged from 17.27 to 58.36 mg/kg against 0.68 mg/kg in controls, that polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons exceeded national limits, and that Bayelsa, Rivers and Delta states are the major spill hotspots. Access: the article is open access in PubMed Central under a CC BY-NC-ND licence; the spill records themselves are not offered by the article page. Coverage is the Niger Delta. Caveats: only the abstract and front matter were read, and sampling details are in the full text. It suits risk assessment and hazard exposure studies of oil pipelines, and no directly related records are catalogued yet.

outcomes: Kernel density mapping of oil spill records identified Bayelsa, Rivers and Delta states as the main hotspots. Soil samples showed total petroleum hydrocarbon of 17.27 to 58.36 mg/kg in impacted soil and 11.73 to 50.78 mg/kg in remediated soil against 0.68 mg/kg in controls, with polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons above the limits of the Department of Petroleum Resources, and pipeline interdiction was found to harm livelihoods and government revenue.
